newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli leaders await corruption probe decision.
newsitem.headline: Israeli leaders await corruption probe decision.

text.p: Israeli prosecutors and police meet on Sunday to decide whether to pursue allegations of high-level corruption which could bring down Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's government.

Asked on television if the government could stay in office if the allegations proved accurate, Internal Security Minister Avigdor Kahalani said: "If the affair is in fact as it appears, at least, there is no doubt that this government has no place."

He said state prosecutor Edna Arbel, the acting attorney general, would meet police to decide whether to approve a full investigation into the government's ill-fated appointment of an attorney general who lasted for just 12 hours.

State-owned Channel One television lit the fuse of the potentially-incendiary affair last week with allegations against Shas party leader Aryeh Deri, a political kingmaker on trial since 1993 on a range of corruption charges.
It said Deri conditioned his party's vital backing for an accord on Israel's withdrawal from the West Bank city of Hebron on the appointment of lawyer Roni Bar-On as attorney general.
It further charged that Deri, an ultra-Orthodox ex-cabinet minister, had won a pledge from Bar-On about a plea bargain that would have enabled him to continue his political career.
Shas, with 10 seats in the 120-member parliament, is a key pillar of Netanyahu's rightist-religious majority.
Bar-On took office two weeks ago and resigned 12 hours later after criticism that he was appointed more for his loyalty to Netanyahu's ruling Likud bloc than for his legal acumen.
Netanyahu, Deri and Bar-On all deny Channel One television's charges and Netanyahu has called for a quick and thorough police investigation into its allegations.
The row has placed considerable heat on the television channel, in the past a frequent target of right-wing criticism as a "nest of leftists."
Channel One news editor Rafik Halabi told Israel Radio on Saturday that he had "spoken documents" to back up the allegations.

Pressed on whether this meant he had recordings of relevant conversations, Halabi said: "You can call this what you want. I call this solid evidence...recorded documents, and more than this I cannot add."
He said he would provide the police with information "within the framework of the law" but he would refuse to disclose the sources of the television reports.
"The moment that a journalist turns over his sources, he has in effect ended his career as a journalist," Halabi said.

Deri's Shas party, though dogged by charges of corruption at many levels, has long had a telling impact on Israeli policy. It has often assisted progress in the Arab-Israeli peace process since formal talks began in 1991.
Shas' two ministers voted in favour 10 days ago when the cabinet decided by 11 votes to 7 to approve the handover of 80 percent of Hebron to Palestinian rule.
The partial withdrawal, carried out the next day, left 20,000 Palestinians in an Israeli-controlled sector where some 400 Jewish settlers and students live in the heart of the violence-plagued town.
